title: Stress, the stress mark and the flow of speech
objectives: I can count the syllables of a Ukrainian word by its vowel letters and find its stressed syllable from the stress mark.
I can explain that unstressed Ukrainian vowels keep their full sound, unlike English ones, except that an unstressed 'е' moves toward 'и' and an unstressed 'и' toward 'е'.
I can explain why the stress of each word and each form must be learned, as in 'рука́' and 'ру́ки', and tell apart words that differ only in stress, such as 'за́мок' and 'замо́к'.
I can choose between 'у' and 'в', 'і' and 'й', and 'з', 'із' and 'зі' from the sounds around them.
I can say how this course writes stress and why ordinary Ukrainian text does not print the mark.

vocabulary.note: Two syllables, stressed on the first: за́-мок. It has exactly the same letters as 'замо́к', lock, and only the stress tells the two words apart. Other forms use the stem 'замк-', with the stress still on the first syllable.

example.source: There is a castle and a lake over there.

vocabulary.note: Two syllables, stressed on the second: за-мо́к. It has the same letters as 'за́мок', castle. Other forms use the stem 'замк-' and are stressed at the end of the word, as in 'замка́'.

example.source: The lock is here, and the key is over there.

vocabulary.note: Stressed on the first syllable. It names a part of the body that does a particular job, such as the nose or the heart, and also an official body with authority, such as a court or a ministry.

example.source: The nose? Yes, it is an organ.

vocabulary.note: Stressed on the second syllable. It is the large musical instrument with pipes, played in churches and concert halls.

example.source: There is a pipe organ in Lviv.

vocabulary.note: Stressed on the last syllable. The form for more than one, 'во́ди', waters, moves the stress to the first syllable.

example.source: The water is here, and the juice is over there.

vocabulary.note: One word for both the leg and the foot, just as 'рука́' covers both the arm and the hand. The stress moves in the form for more than one: 'но́ги', legs.

example.source: This is a leg, and this is an arm.

vocabulary.note: Stressed on the first syllable. The form for more than one, 'слова́', words, moves the stress to the last syllable.

example.source: This is a word, and this is a book.

vocabulary.note: Three syllables, мо-ло-ко́, stressed on the last. Every 'о' keeps its full [ɔ], although only the last one is stressed.

example.source: The milk and the cheese are here.

vocabulary.note: Three syllables, о́-зе-ро, stressed on the first. The form for more than one, 'озе́ра', lakes, moves the stress onto the 'е', where it is heard clearly.

example.source: Here is a lake, and over there is a town.

vocabulary.note: Stressed on the first syllable. The stress stays there in the form for more than one, 'кни́ги', books.

example.source: The book is here, and the pen is over there.

vocabulary.note: Five syllables, у-ні-вер-си-те́т, stressed on the last. The first 'е' is unstressed and moves toward 'и'; the last 'е' is stressed and clear.

example.source: The university and the post office are over there.

vocabulary.note: Stressed on the first syllable. It is also the handle of a door or a bag. It is built from 'рука́', hand: the 'к' of 'рука́' becomes 'ч', and an added 'к' makes a word for something small, so its parts mean 'little hand'.

example.source: This is a pen, and this is a pencil.

vocabulary.note: Stressed on the last syllable. Other forms drop the 'е' of the last syllable and keep the stress at the end of the word, as in 'олівця́'.

example.source: There is a book and a pencil here.

vocabulary.note: Stressed on the first syllable. Like 'сього́дні', today, it often opens a sentence.

One syllable, so it has no stress mark. After a vowel and before a consonant it becomes 'в', which has no vowel and makes no syllable; the note on euphony gives the rules. The noun after it changes its ending ('шко́ла', 'у шко́лі') for a reason unit 5 explains.
The form of 'і' used after a vowel, except before 'й', 'я', 'ю', 'є' and 'ї'. It has no vowel of its own, so it joins the syllable before it: 'ма́ма й та́то' runs on as [ˈmɑmɑj ˈtɑtɔ].
The usual form; 'із' and 'зі' replace it where 'з' alone would be hard to say. The noun after it changes its ending ('Ки́їв', 'з Ки́єва') for a reason unit 5 explains.

dialogues.title: Reading the signs
dialogues.context: Sam and his teacher Iryna Petrivna walk past the buildings near the university. Street signs print no stress marks, so Sam asks what each one says and listens for the stressed syllable; the marks in the Ukrainian text show what he hears. 'Кни́ги' is the form of 'кни́га' for more than one book, and its stress stays on the first syllable.

lines.speaker: Сем
lines.source: The post office. And over there?

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.source: Over there are a café and a school.

dialogues.title: A castle and a lock
dialogues.context: Oksana and Taras spend a day at an old castle by a lake. On the door of a tower hangs a heavy lock, and its key hangs at the ticket office. In 'А у Льво́ві' the form 'у' is used even after a vowel, because 'у' is always used before 'льв'.

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.target: Так, це за́мок. А там о́зеро.
lines.source: Yes, this is the castle. And over there is the lake.
lines.source_literal: yes, this castle. and there lake

lines.speaker: Окса́на
lines.source: Today the castle, and tomorrow Lviv.

lines.speaker: Тара́с
lines.source: And is there a castle in Lviv?

dialogues.title: Coffee with milk, tea with sugar
dialogues.context: Oksana brings Sam to Andrii's café. Listen for 'з' after a vowel in 'ка́ва з молоко́м' and for 'із' between two consonants in 'чай із цу́кром'. After these words 'молоко́' and 'цу́кор' change their endings, for a reason unit 5 explains.

lines.speaker: Андрі́й
lines.target: Ка́ва з молоко́м і чай із цу́кром.
lines.source: A coffee with milk and a tea with sugar.

lines.speaker: Андрі́й
lines.target: А сього́дні є сир і хліб.
lines.source: And today there is cheese and bread.
lines.source_literal: and today there-is cheese and bread

grammar.title: Syllables, the stressed syllable and the stress mark
grammar.explanation:
A syllable is one beat of a word: a vowel sound with the consonants grouped around it. English 'banana' has three syllables, ba-na-na. In Ukrainian you count syllables by counting vowel letters, because every vowel letter makes one syllable and every syllable has exactly one vowel letter. The ten vowel letters are:

- 'а', 'е', 'и', 'і', 'о', 'у'
- 'я', 'ю', 'є', 'ї'

'Й', 'ь' and the apostrophe are not vowels, so they add no syllable. 'Я', 'ю', 'є' and 'ї' count once each, even where they write [j] plus a vowel. So 'чай' has one syllable, 'ма́ма' has two (ма́-ма), 'молоко́' three (мо-ло-ко́) and 'Украї́на' four (У-кра-ї́-на).

In every word of two or more syllables, one syllable is stressed: it is said louder and a little longer than the others. The other syllables are unstressed. English works the same way: 'banana' is stressed on its second syllable.

Unlike English, Ukrainian keeps the sound of its unstressed vowels. In English 'banana' the two unstressed vowels weaken to a short 'uh'. In Ukrainian 'молоко́', milk, all three 'о's are the same full [ɔ], and only the last is louder and longer; in 'ма́ма' both vowels are [ɑ]. Say every vowel clearly, and let loudness and length alone show the stress.

Two vowels are the exception. An unstressed 'е' moves toward 'и', and an unstressed 'и' moves toward 'е', so that in quick speech the two can sound almost alike:

- 'сестра́', sister: the unstressed 'е' sounds a little like 'и'
- 'зима́', winter: the unstressed 'и' sounds a little like 'е'

Under stress each keeps its own sound: 'ве́чір', evening, has a clear [ɛ], and 'ри́ба', fish, a clear [ɪ]. Because the unstressed pair can sound alike, Ukrainians check the spelling in another form of the word where that vowel is stressed: 'се́стри', sisters, shows the 'е' of 'сестра́', and 'зи́ми', winters, shows the 'и' of 'зима́'.

This course writes the stress with a mark, a small stroke over the stressed vowel: 'ма́ма', 'вода́'. The mark stands on every word of two or more syllables, in Ukrainian sentences and in Ukrainian words quoted in English, and on capital letters too: 'О́зеро там.' A word of one syllable has no mark, because there is no choice of syllable for a mark to show: 'чай', 'кіт', 'Львів'. The mark only shows the stress; it does not change the sound of the vowel.

Ordinary Ukrainian text does not print the mark. Books, newspapers, signs and websites leave it out, because readers already know the stress of the words they read. Dictionaries and books for young children and for learners print it, and an ordinary text occasionally marks a single word whose meaning depends on its stress, such as the pairs in the third note. You therefore learn the stress of each word together with the word, and this course marks it for that reason. You do not need to type the mark in your answers: the apps accept an answer with or without it.

rows: three vowel letters, each a full [ɔ]
'ї' is one vowel letter, though it writes [ji]
the apostrophe is not a vowel
'й' is not a vowel, so one syllable
'ь' is not a vowel, so one syllable

examples.source: There is a lake over there.
The fish and the cheese are here.

grammar.title: Free and mobile stress
grammar.explanation:
In some languages the stress always falls on the same syllable of a word, for example the first, so a reader can predict it. Ukrainian stress is free: it can fall on any syllable, and nothing in the spelling tells you which.

- On the first syllable: 'ма́ма', 'кни́га', 'о́зеро', 'за́втра'
- On a middle syllable: 'Окса́на', 'сього́дні', 'Украї́на'
- On the last syllable: 'вода́', 'молоко́', 'оліве́ць', 'університе́т'

Ukrainian stress is also mobile: in another form of the same word it can move to another syllable. The clearest case at this stage is the plural, the form of a noun (a word that names a person, place or thing) that names more than one thing, as opposed to the singular, the form that names one. 'Рука́' is one hand and 'ру́ки' is hands. English does not move the stress between forms of one word ('book', 'books'); it does so only between related words, such as 'PHOtograph' and 'phoTOgraphy'. Ukrainian does it within one word, in either direction:

- 'рука́', hand, and 'ру́ки', hands
- 'нога́', leg, and 'но́ги', legs
- 'голова́', head, and 'го́лови', heads
- 'сестра́', sister, and 'се́стри', sisters
- 'вікно́', window, and 'ві́кна', windows
- 'мі́сто', city, and 'міста́', cities

Many other words keep their stress in every form: 'кни́га', book, and 'кни́ги', books; 'ма́ма', mom, and 'ма́ми', moms. No rule tells you in advance which words move. The habit that works is simple: learn the stress of a word together with the word, and learn the stress of each new form when a table in this course shows it, just as you learn a spelling. Unit 5 explains how plurals and the other forms are made; here notice only that the stress can move.

Mobile stress is also what makes the spelling check of the first note possible: 'се́стри' moves the stress onto the 'е' of 'сестра́', so you can hear which letter to write.

grammar.title: Words told apart by stress
grammar.explanation:
Because Ukrainian stress is free, two different words can have exactly the same letters and differ only in which syllable is stressed. Each is a separate word with its own meaning, and in speech the stress is the only thing that tells them apart:

- 'за́мок', castle, stressed on the first syllable, and 'замо́к', lock, stressed on the second
- 'о́рган', an organ of the body or an official body with authority, stressed on the first syllable, and 'орга́н', the musical instrument with pipes, stressed on the second

English has a few such pairs too: 'DEsert', a dry land, and 'deSERT', to abandon; 'REcord', a disc, and 'reCORD', to capture sound.

In ordinary Ukrainian text, where no mark is printed, the rest of the sentence decides: a sentence about towers and walls is about 'за́мок', and a sentence about a key or a door is about 'замо́к'. When you speak, give each word its own stress, or the listener may hear the other word.

The recordings in this course are made by a speech engine from the text without the stress mark, so they may say both words of a pair alike. For these pairs, trust the mark rather than the recording; this course never tests them by listening or dictation.

examples.source: The lock and the key are here.
Today the castle, and tomorrow the lake.

grammar.title: Euphony: 'у' and 'в', 'і' and 'й', 'з', 'із' and 'зі'
grammar.explanation:
Ukrainian likes speech to flow, with vowels and consonants taking turns. It avoids two vowels meeting where one word ends and the next begins, and it avoids a long pile of consonants. For this reason a few very short words have two or three forms, and the sounds around them decide which form you say and write. English does the same with 'a' and 'an': 'a pear', 'an apple'. Ukrainian grammar calls this 'милозву́чність', literally 'pleasant-sound-ness', in English euphony.

The forms 'в' and 'й' have no vowel, so they make no syllable of their own and join the syllable next to them. In 'Окса́на в шко́лі', Oksana is at school, the 'в' is the [w] of 'cow', said at the end of '-на': [ɔkˈsɑnɑw ˈʃkɔlʲi]. 'Окса́на й Тара́с' runs on in the same way with [j]. The forms with a vowel, 'у', 'і', 'із' and 'зі', make a syllable of their own and break up a group of consonants.

'У' and 'в' mean 'in', 'at' or 'to'. Use 'у':

- between two consonants: 'Тара́с у шко́лі', Taras is at school
- at the start of a sentence or after a comma, before a consonant: 'У Ки́єві зима́.', It is winter in Kyiv.
- always before 'в' and 'ф', and before 'льв', 'св', 'тв' and 'хв', even after a vowel: 'Сестра́ у Льво́ві.', My sister is in Lviv.

Use 'в':

- after a vowel, before a consonant: 'Окса́на в шко́лі', Oksana is at school
- between two vowels: 'Окса́на в Украї́ні', Oksana is in Ukraine
- at the start of a sentence, before a vowel: 'В Украї́ні зима́.', It is winter in Ukraine.

'І' and 'й' both mean 'and'. Use 'і':

- after a consonant: 'Тара́с і Окса́на', 'хліб і сир'
- before a word that begins with 'й', 'я', 'ю', 'є' or 'ї', whose [j] would merge with 'й': 'Окса́на і я', Oksana and I
- at the start of a sentence and after a comma

Use 'й':

- after a vowel, before a consonant: 'Окса́на й Тара́с', 'ка́ва й чай'
- between two vowels: 'Окса́на й Іри́на'

'З', 'із' and 'зі' mean 'from' or 'with'. 'З' is the usual form: 'ка́ва з молоко́м', coffee with milk; 'Окса́на з Ки́єва', Oksana is from Kyiv. Before a voiceless consonant, such as 'к', 'п', 'т' or 'х', 'з' partly loses its voice and sounds between [z] and [s]: 'з Ки́єва', from Kyiv. This is one of the exceptions to the rule of unit 2 that a voiced consonant stays voiced before another consonant. Use 'із' between two consonants where 'з' alone would be hard to say, especially before 'з', 'с', 'ц', 'ч', 'ш' and 'щ': 'чай із цу́кром', tea with sugar; 'Тара́с із Се́мом', Taras with Sam. Use 'зі' before 'з', 'с', 'ш' or 'щ' followed by another consonant, and before 'мн': 'зі шко́ли', from school; 'зі мно́ю', with me.

The word after these short words often changes its ending: 'шко́ла' becomes 'у шко́лі' and 'зі шко́ли', 'молоко́' becomes 'з молоко́м', and 'Ки́їв' becomes 'з Ки́єва'. Unit 5 explains why. Until then, learn these phrases whole:

- 'у шко́лі', at school
- 'зі шко́ли', from school
- 'в Украї́ні', in Ukraine
- 'у Льво́ві', in Lviv
- 'у Ки́єві', in Kyiv
- 'з Ки́єва', from Kyiv
- 'ка́ва з молоко́м', coffee with milk
- 'чай із цу́кром', tea with sugar
- 'із Се́мом', with Sam
- 'зі мно́ю', with me

These choices are the standard of careful speech and writing, and every Ukrainian sentence in this course follows them; in casual speech people do not always keep to them.

rows: at the start, before a consonant
after a vowel, before a consonant
between vowels; at the start, before a vowel

examples.source: Oksana and Taras are over there.

culture.title: Stress in names, and a melodious language
culture.text:
Place names are where a visitor first notices Ukrainian stress. Ukrainians stress the names of their largest cities like this:

- 'Ки́їв', Kyiv, on the first syllable
- 'Ха́рків', Kharkiv, on the first syllable
- 'Оде́са', Odesa, on the second syllable
- 'Дніпро́', Dnipro, on the last syllable
- 'Львів', Lviv, a single syllable

Personal names are stressed with the same care. The national poet Taras Shevchenko is 'Тара́с Шевче́нко', with the stress on the second syllable of both names, and 'Окса́на' and 'Іри́на' are also stressed on the second syllable. A Ukrainian will understand a name said with the wrong stress, but will notice it at once.

Dictionaries of Ukrainian pronunciation record the stress of every word and of its forms, and radio and television presenters are expected to follow them. Words that many people stress wrongly, such as 'кіломе́тр', kilometer, and 'листопа́д', November, appear in popular lists and quizzes, and looking up a stress in a dictionary is an ordinary habit, even among native speakers.

Ukrainians often call their language 'солов’ї́на мо́ва', literally 'nightingale's language', for its melodious sound. The euphony rules of this unit are part of that sound. Schoolchildren learn the choice between 'у' and 'в' and between 'і' and 'й' as part of what Ukrainian grammar calls 'милозву́чність', euphony, and poets and songwriters use the shorter and longer forms to fit their lines to the rhythm of a verse.

exercises.explanation: Count the vowel letters: мо-ло-ко́ has three 'о's, so it has three syllables.

exercises.prompt: Match the Ukrainian with the English
exercises.explanation: Three of these words are stressed on the last syllable ('вода́', 'нога́', 'оліве́ць') and three on the first.

exercises.prompt: Why does 'чай' have no stress mark?
choices: 'Й' is a vowel, so the stress always falls on it.
It has one vowel letter, so it has only one syllable.
The mark is left off every word that ends in a consonant.
exercises.explanation: 'Й' is a consonant, so 'чай' has one vowel letter and one syllable. A word of one syllable needs no mark.

choices: There is a lake over there.
There is a castle over there.
There is a university over there.
exercises.explanation: 'О́зеро', lake, is stressed on the first syllable, and its final unstressed 'о' keeps its full [ɔ].
The mark stands on 'ї', the third of four vowel letters: У-кра-ї́-на.

exercises.hint_source: Here is the pen, and there is the pencil.
exercises.explanation: The word for pencil is stressed on its last syllable: о-лі-ве́ць.

exercises.prompt: In 'молоко́' only the last 'о' is stressed. How are the other two said?
choices: As a short 'uh', like the unstressed vowels of English 'banana'
As the same full [ɔ], only quieter and shorter
Not at all: they are silent
exercises.explanation: Ukrainian unstressed vowels keep their sound. Only loudness and length mark the stressed syllable.

exercises.prompt: In 'сестра́' the 'е' is unstressed. How does it sound?
exercises.explanation: An unstressed 'е' moves toward 'и', and an unstressed 'и' moves toward 'е'. Under stress each keeps its own sound.

exercises.prompt: Match each word with its meaning
exercises.explanation: Each pair has the same letters; only the stressed syllable differs.
'Замо́к', stressed on the second syllable, is a lock. 'За́мок', stressed on the first, is a castle, and a key is 'ключ'.

exercises.prompt: 'Рука́' is one hand and 'ру́ки' is hands. What does this pair show?
choices: Stress can move to another syllable in another form of the same word.
'Ру́ки' is a different word with another meaning.
The form for more than one always moves the stress to the first syllable.
exercises.explanation: Ukrainian stress is mobile. It can also move the other way: 'мі́сто', city, and 'міста́', cities.

exercises.prompt: Can you work out the stress of a new Ukrainian word from its spelling?
choices: Yes: it always falls on the first syllable.
Yes: it always falls on the second-to-last syllable.
No: it can fall on any syllable, so you learn it with each word and each form.
exercises.explanation: Ukrainian stress is free: 'ма́ма' is stressed on the first syllable, 'Окса́на' on the second and 'молоко́' on the last.

exercises.prompt: How can you check that 'сестра́' is written with 'е' and not 'и'?
choices: Find the form 'се́стри', sisters, where that vowel is stressed and clear.
Write 'и', because every unstressed vowel is written 'и'.
exercises.explanation: An unstressed 'е' and 'и' can sound alike, so you check the vowel in a form where it carries the stress.
'З Ки́єва' is 'from Kyiv'; 'in Kyiv' would be 'у Ки́єві'.

exercises.prompt: Which form begins the sentence '___ Украї́ні зима́.', meaning 'It is winter in Ukraine'?
exercises.explanation: At the start of a sentence, before a vowel, the form is 'в': 'В Украї́ні зима́.' Before a consonant it would be 'у', as in 'У Ки́єві зима́.'
After a vowel and before a consonant the form is 'в', said [w], which joins the syllable before it.
'У' is always used before 'льв', even after a vowel, because 'в' before 'льв' would pile up consonants.
After a vowel and before a consonant, 'and' is 'й'.

exercises.hint_source: Taras and Olena are over there.
exercises.explanation: After a consonant, 'and' is 'і', which makes a syllable of its own.

exercises.prompt: Which form of 'and' completes 'Окса́на ___ я тут.', meaning 'Oksana and I are here'?
exercises.explanation: Before a word that begins with 'я', 'and' is 'і', even after a vowel: the [j] of 'й' would merge with the [j] of 'я'.
Between two consonants, before 'с', the form is 'із', which breaks up the consonants with a vowel.

exercises.prompt: Why is 'from school' 'зі шко́ли' and not 'з' alone?
choices: 'Зі' is used before every word that begins with 'ш'.
'Шко́ли' begins with 'ш' plus another consonant, and 'зі' keeps the consonants from piling up.
exercises.explanation: 'Зі' stands before 'з', 'с', 'ш' or 'щ' followed by another consonant, and before 'мн', as in 'зі мно́ю'.
'Ка́ва' is coffee and 'з молоко́м' is with milk; tea with sugar would be 'чай із цу́кром'.

exercises.prompt_source: Oksana and Taras are at school.
exercises.explanation: 'Й' follows the vowel at the end of 'Окса́на', and 'у' stands between the consonants of 'Тара́с' and 'шко́лі'; 'в' would need a vowel before it.

exercises.prompt_source: Tea with sugar and coffee with milk.
exercises.explanation: 'Із' stands between the consonants of 'чай' and 'цу́кром', 'і' follows the consonant of 'цу́кром', and 'з' follows the vowel of 'ка́ва'.

exercises.prompt_source: Today Kyiv, and tomorrow the castle.
exercises.explanation: 'А' joins the two contrasting parts. The castle is 'за́мок', stressed on the first syllable; 'замо́к', stressed on the second, is a lock.
Before 'я' the word for 'and' is 'і', even after the vowel of 'ма́ма'. After 'я' and before the consonant of 'ма́ма' it is 'й'.

exercises.prompt_source: The lake is over there, and the castle is here.
exercises.explanation: 'А' joins two contrasting statements. The castle is 'за́мок', stressed on the first syllable.

exercises.prompt_source: Taras and I are in Lviv.
exercises.explanation: In the first answer 'і' follows the consonant of 'Тара́с' and stands before 'я'; in the second 'й' follows the vowel of 'я' and stands before the consonant of 'Тара́с'. 'У' is always used before 'льв'.

exercises.hint_source: The pen and the pencil are here.
exercises.explanation: 'Й' stands between two vowels, the 'а' of 'ру́чка' and the 'о' of 'оліве́ць'.

exercises.hint_source: Over there are a café and a school.
exercises.explanation: After the vowel at the end of 'кафе́' and before the consonant of 'шко́ла', 'and' is 'й'.
